title: Operator-language Feynman rules for driven-dissipative quantum systems: from mean field to non-Gaussian photon correlations
authors: Peter Ehlers, Phi Hung Nguyen, Daniel Soh
abstract: We construct Feynman rules for Lindblad master equations in the operator language of quantum optics: a fixed algebra of elementary operator moves and closed-form propagators for perturbation theory about an exactly solvable, in most cases Gaussian, generator. The expansion separates into a kinematic part (the shift algebra on the Wick-ordered eigenoperators $O_{mn}=:(c^\dagger)^m c^n:$, from which the vertex table for a specified interaction is assembled) and a dynamical part that enters only through the resolvent of the unperturbed generator, diagonal and additive for any stable, diagonalizable Gaussian $L_0$, including thermal and squeezed reservoirs and correlated decay, and equally available for a two-level emitter, driven or undriven. In the driven Kerr cavity the loop expansion is the semiclassical expansion and the series is asymptotic. In a strongly driven two-level atom, dressed lines replace a series of finite radius by one accurate deep into saturation, one line per Mollow component. For Kerr rings and chains the cost is polynomial in the number of sites at fixed perturbative order. On a three-site ring the diagrams recover the non-Gaussian part of the three-photon correlation that the Gaussian cumulant closure lacks; carried to tenth order they give the smallest $g^{(3)}$ error of the methods compared for $U\leq0.25κ$ at a cost below that of a fourth-order closure, and third- and fourth-order closures are more accurate at moderate coupling. The same rules, extended to the counting-field-tilted generator, give the photon-counting cumulants of a disordered eight-site chain beyond direct diagonalization; quantum-jump trajectories at three couplings agree with them to within $1.6$ standard errors, within one at the strongest coupling, where they place the third cumulant six standard errors above the Gaussian value.
summary: This paper introduces a novel, operator-language Feynman rule set for analyzing driven-dissipative quantum systems governed by Lindblad master equations. By systematically separating the generator into a solvable part and an interaction part, it allows for diagrammatic calculation of correlation functions. This method is particularly valuable for accurately determining non-Gaussian statistics in complex quantum optical setups.
main_problem: The paper develops a systematic, diagrammatic perturbation theory to construct Feynman rules for Lindblad master equations governing driven-dissipative quantum systems.
main_result: The rules successfully calculate non-Gaussian photon correlations (like $g^{(3)}$) in systems like Kerr rings, surpassing the accuracy of standard Gaussian cumulant closures.
method: The method constructs rules by splitting the Liouvillian generator $L = L_0 + L_{	ext{int}}$, separating the expansion into a kinematic part (algebraic contractions) and a dynamical part (the resolvent of the solvable unperturbed generator $L_0$).
model_or_system: The theory applies to open quantum systems described by Lindblad master equations, covering diverse models such as driven Kerr cavities, strongly driven two-level atoms, and coupled Kerr chains/rings.
key_observables: Photon correlations ($g^{(2)}, g^{(3)}$), photon-counting cumulants, and steady-state expectation values.
important_parameters: Coupling strengths ($U, \kappa$), detunings ($\Delta$), and the order of the perturbative expansion.
main_assumptions: The method assumes the existence of an exactly solvable, Gaussian unperturbed generator $L_0$ whose resolvent can be calculated in closed form.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the construction process, showing the splitting of the generator, the kinematic rules, and the resulting diagrammatic structure used to calculate observables.
paper_structure: The paper builds the formalism by defining the operator language for the Liouvillian, detailing the separation into kinematic and dynamic parts, and then applies these rules to calculate specific observables for various physical models, comparing results against known limits and closures.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, systematic, and diagrammatic framework for calculating higher-order correlations in open quantum systems, moving beyond the limitations of mean-field or Gaussian approximations.
